simple: how long you wait from asking for something until it arrives.
analogy: the time of one round trip of the helper to the pantry.
precise: the time between issuing a memory request (for example a load) and the moment its data can be used; measured in seconds (ns) or in processor clock cycles.
source: D1 of F1-32 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-32 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much data arrives per second once it is flowing.
analogy: how many sacks per minute the corridor can carry.
precise: the rate of data transfer, in bytes per second (GB/s = 109 bytes per second in this course); also called throughput when it describes a measured rate.
source: D2 of F1-32 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D3 of F1-32 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: several layers of storage, from tiny and fast to huge and slow.
analogy: cutting board, shelves by the stove, shelf along the wall, back room, pantry, warehouse across town.
precise: the organisation of a computer's storage into levels (registers, caches, main memory, storage) in which each level is larger, slower and cheaper per byte than the one above it, and holds copies of data used by the level above.
source: D1 of F1-32 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-32 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small fast memory that keeps copies of data you used recently.
analogy: the shelves near the stove.
precise: a small, fast memory, managed by hardware, that holds copies of blocks of main memory so that later accesses to them are served quickly; F1-33 explains its organisation.
source: D1 of F1-32 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-32 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the data a program keeps using during one phase of its work.
analogy: the jars a dish needs this evening.
precise: the set of memory locations (or its size in bytes) that a program accesses repeatedly during an interval of time; whether it fits in a cache level decides that level's hit rate.
source: D1 of F1-32 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: to keep stuff arriving fast while each trip is slow, many trips must be under way at once.
analogy: forty sacks per minute with a five-minute walk means two hundred sacks must be on the way at any moment.
precise: in a steady system, the average number of items in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside; for memory, bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency.
source: D3 of F1-32 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: several memory requests waiting at the same time instead of one after another.
analogy: several helpers walking the corridor together.
precise: the number of outstanding memory accesses a processor can have at once; it needs independent addresses, because a load whose address depends on another load cannot start until that load returns.
source: D3 of F1-32 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: fetching data before it is asked for, by guessing what comes next.
analogy: a helper who notices you take jars from left to right and brings the next one early.
precise: starting a memory transfer before the program's own access, either by instructions in the program (software prefetch) or by hardware that detects patterns such as fixed strides (hardware prefetch).
source: D1 of F1-32 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-32 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the fixed-size chunk of memory a cache always moves and stores as one piece.
analogy: a whole tray of neighbouring jars.
precise: the unit of storage and transfer of a cache (also called a cache block): an aligned group of 2b consecutive bytes of memory; the build container reports 64-byte lines (Listing 4).
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-33 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a hit means the data was already in the cache; a miss means it had to be fetched.
analogy: the tray is on the shelf, or someone must walk to the pantry.
precise: an access is a hit if the cache holds a valid line whose tag matches the address; otherwise it is a miss and the line is fetched from the next level; hit rate = hits ÷ accesses.
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-33 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: three parts of an address: which byte in the line, which set, and a label to tell lines apart.
analogy: the jar's place on the tray, the shelf section, and the label written on the tray.
precise: for a cache with 2s sets and 2b-byte lines, the low b bits of an address are the block offset, the next s bits the set index, and the remaining high bits the tag stored with the line.
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-33 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the group of places where one particular line is allowed to live.
analogy: one numbered shelf section.
precise: a group of E line slots selected by the set index; a line can be stored only in the set its address selects.
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one slot inside a set.
analogy: one tray slot in a section.
precise: one of the E line slots of every set; a cache with E slots per set is E-way set-associative, and its associativity is E.
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-33 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every line has exactly one place it may go.
analogy: sections with room for one tray each.
precise: a cache with one line per set (E = 1).
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every line has a few places it may go, all in one set.
analogy: sections with room for several trays.
precise: a cache with S sets of E > 1 lines; lookup compares the tag with all E lines of the selected set in parallel.
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-33 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: any line may go anywhere.
analogy: one big section where any tray fits in any slot.
precise: a cache with a single set (S = 1); there are no index bits and every lookup compares the tag with every line.
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when a set is full, throw out the line used longest ago.
analogy: the tray nobody touched for the longest time goes back to the pantry.
precise: least-recently-used replacement: on a miss to a full set, the victim is the line whose last access is oldest; hardware often approximates it (pseudo-LRU).
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-33 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a miss that happens only because too many lines want the same set, even though the cache has room elsewhere.
analogy: section 0 overflows while sections 1–63 stand half empty.
precise: a miss that would not occur in a fully associative cache of the same size; one of the "three Cs" with compulsory and capacity misses (F1-34).
source: D1 of F1-33 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-33 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: if you used something a moment ago, you will probably use it again soon.
analogy: Lina's salt, oil and pepper.
precise: the tendency of a program to access the same memory location again within a short time; caches exploit it by keeping recently used lines.
source: D1 of F1-34 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-34 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: if you used something, you will probably use its neighbours soon.
analogy: Kofi using every jar on the tray.
precise: the tendency of a program to access locations near recently accessed ones; caches exploit it by moving whole lines.
source: D1 of F1-34 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-34 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far apart, in elements, two accesses in a row are.
analogy: Tomás taking one jar from each tray.
precise: in a stride-k reference pattern a program accesses every k-th element of a sequence; stride 1 is sequential access.
source: D1 of F1-34 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the miss you cannot avoid the first time you touch a line.
analogy: the first trip for a tray that was never on the shelf.
precise: a miss on the first access to a line (a cold miss); it occurs even in an infinitely large cache.
source: D1 of F1-34 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-34 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a miss because the cache is too small for what you are using.
analogy: the shelf is full, so a tray you will need again goes back.
precise: a miss that would occur even in a fully associative cache of the same size, because the working set is larger than the cache.
source: D1 of F1-34 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-34 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a table or 3-D chart of read speed for many sizes and strides.
analogy: a map of how fast each helper can work for every size of order and every way of picking jars.
precise: the read throughput of a stride benchmark as a function of working-set size and stride; its ridges show the cache levels, its slopes show spatial locality.
source: D1 of F1-34 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a table stored row by row: first all of row 0, then all of row 1.
analogy: trays lined up row after row in the pantry.
precise: the layout in which element [i][j] of an n-column array is stored at position i × n + j; C and C++ arrays use it.
source: D1 of F1-34 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D6 of F1-34 (ISO/IEC 14882 (C++ standard draft)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every write goes to the cache and to the next level at once.
analogy: Ravi correcting the pantry book after every spoon.
precise: a write-hit policy in which a store updates the cached line and is also sent to the next level of the hierarchy, so the lower level always holds the current value.
source: D1 of F1-35 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-35 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: writes stay in the cache; the next level is updated only when the line leaves.
analogy: Mei's red sticker, book corrected when the tray goes back.
precise: a write-hit policy in which a store updates only the cached line and marks it dirty; the whole line is written to the next level when it is evicted (or explicitly flushed).
source: D1 of F1-35 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-35 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a flag that says "this line was changed and memory does not know yet".
analogy: the red sticker on the tray.
precise: a status bit per cache line, set by a store in a write-back cache; a dirty victim must be written back before its slot is reused, a clean one may be dropped.
source: D1 of F1-35 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-35 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: on a write miss, first bring the line into the cache, then write it there.
analogy: fetching the tray before changing a jar on it.
precise: a write-miss policy that loads the missing line into the cache and then performs the write as a hit; usually paired with write-back.
source: D1 of F1-35 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-35 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: on a write miss, send the write onward and do not load the line.
analogy: correcting the pantry book directly without bringing the tray.
precise: a write-miss policy (also called write-around) that passes the write to the next level without allocating a line; usually paired with write-through.
source: D1 of F1-35 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-35 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small queue where writes wait so the processor does not have to.
analogy: an outbox tray by the kitchen door that a runner empties.
precise: a buffer between a cache and the next level that holds pending writes (or written-back lines) so that the processor can continue while they drain; reads may need to check it.
source: D2 of F1-35 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D3 of F1-35 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making sure all cores see one agreed value for each memory location, even though each has its own cache.
analogy: the kitchen rule about recipe copies.
precise: the property that, for each memory location, at any time either one core may write it or any number of cores may read it (single-writer–multiple-reader), and every read returns the value of the most recent write to that location.
source: D4 of F1-36 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D3 of F1-36 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a set of four labels each cache keeps for each line, and rules for changing them.
analogy: each cook's copy is marked "mine and changed", "mine only", "shared" or "torn up".
precise: an invalidation-based coherence protocol with line states Modified (only copy, dirty), Exclusive (only copy, clean), Shared (clean, possibly in other caches) and Invalid.
source: D4 of F1-36 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D2 of F1-36 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every cache listens to every other cache's requests.
analogy: every cook hears every call across the kitchen.
precise: a family of coherence protocols in which coherence requests are broadcast to all caches (over a bus or another ordered interconnect) and each cache controller reacts to the requests that concern lines it holds.
source: D4 of F1-36 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D3 of F1-36 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a record that says which caches have a copy of which line.
analogy: a list on the pantry door of who holds a copy of each recipe.
precise: a structure, usually distributed with memory, that tracks the state and the sharers of each line, so coherence requests can be sent only to the caches involved instead of broadcast.
source: D4 of F1-36 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D3 of F1-36 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: telling other caches their copy is no longer valid.
analogy: "tear up your copies!"
precise: a coherence action that changes other caches' copies of a line to Invalid, so that a core can obtain write permission (single writer).
source: D4 of F1-36 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two threads slow each other down by writing different variables that happen to share one cache line.
analogy: two recipes printed on one sheet.
precise: coherence traffic caused by independent data items located in the same line; because coherence works per line, writes to either item invalidate the other core's copy of the whole line.
source: D1 of F1-36 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-36 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rules for which values loads may return when several cores read and write memory.
analogy: the kitchen's rules for when a note counts as "on the board".
precise: a specification of the allowed behaviours of a multithreaded program's loads and stores, across all memory locations, as defined for a hardware architecture or a programming language.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the result is as if all threads took turns, one memory operation at a time, each in program order.
analogy: one pen on a chain at the board; every cook writes and reads only with it.
precise: a model in which the result of any execution equals some single total order of all memory operations that respects each thread's program order (SC).
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D3 of F1-37 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small queue in each core where finished stores wait before they are written to the cache.
analogy: each cook's outbox tray.
precise: a per-core FIFO of committed stores not yet written to the coherent cache; the core's own loads check it first (forwarding), while other cores cannot see its contents.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a model like SC except that a load may be done before an earlier store to another address.
analogy: notes may wait in the outbox while the cook already reads the board.
precise: TSO relaxes only the store→load order of SC (for different addresses), as a FIFO store buffer does; stores from all cores still appear in one total order.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tiny multi-thread program used to ask "can this outcome happen?"
analogy: the two-cooks-one-pot story, written down exactly.
precise: a short program with a few threads and an outcome of interest; a model either allows or forbids the outcome.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an instruction that stops later memory operations from overtaking earlier ones.
analogy: "pin it up and wait before you look".
precise: an instruction (or language construct) that orders memory operations before it with those after it; on a TSO machine, a full fence drains the store buffer before later loads execute.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D7 of F1-37 (Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one-way orderings: a release store keeps earlier work before it, an acquire load keeps later work after it.
analogy: "finish the dish, then flip the ready sign" / "see the sign, then pick up the dish".
precise: in C++, a release store that is read by an acquire load synchronises with it, so writes before the release happen-before reads after the acquire; it does not order a release store with a later acquire load to a different variable.
source: D6 of F1-37 (ISO/IEC 14882 (C++ standard draft)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: each program uses its own made-up addresses, and the hardware and operating system map them to real memory.
analogy: ingredient names instead of shelf numbers.
precise: a mechanism in which a program's addresses (virtual addresses) are translated, page by page, to physical addresses through tables maintained by the operating system, giving each process its own address space, protection and the ability to map pages on demand.
source: D1 of F1-38 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-38 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fixed-size block of memory, the unit of mapping.
analogy: a pantry box.
precise: an aligned, power-of-two-sized block of virtual address space (4096 bytes on the build container) mapped as a unit onto a physical frame of the same size.
source: D1 of F1-38 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the table that says where each page really is.
analogy: the index binder.
precise: an in-memory data structure, per address space, mapping virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers plus permission and status bits; on x86-64 a tree of 512-entry tables.
source: D1 of F1-38 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D7 of F1-38 (Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: following the tables from the top to find one page's location.
analogy: leafing through the binder's four tabbed sections.
precise: the sequence of memory reads, one per table level, that the hardware (or software) performs to translate a virtual page number when the TLB has no entry for it.
source: D1 of F1-38 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-38 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tiny cache of recent address translations.
analogy: the sticky notes at the station.
precise: the translation lookaside buffer: a small, associative cache of page-table entries indexed by virtual page number, checked on every memory access; a miss starts a page-table walk.
source: D1 of F1-38 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D2 of F1-38 (Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the hardware finds no valid mapping and asks the operating system to fix it.
analogy: the binder has no entry yet; the manager fetches a box.
precise: an exception raised when translation finds a missing or forbidden mapping; the kernel either maps a page (a minor fault when no disk read is needed, a major fault when it is) and restarts the instruction, or signals an error.
source: D1 of F1-38 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D8 of F1-38 (Linux kernel documentation and man-pages) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a much larger page, so one translation covers more memory.
analogy: one sticky note for a whole shelf instead of one box.
precise: a page larger than the base size (2 MiB on x86-64, mapped by a level-2 entry), which reduces TLB misses and walk depth; Linux offers them through transparent huge pages and explicit huge-page pools.
source: D7 of F1-38 (Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3); D8 of F1-38 (Linux kernel documentation and man-pages) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much memory the TLB can cover at once.
analogy: number of sticky notes times what each note covers.
precise: number of TLB entries × page size; a working set larger than the reach causes TLB misses even if its data fits in the caches.
source: D3 of F1-38 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach"); D1 of F1-38 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the main memory chips: dense and cheap, but slow and needing constant refreshing.
analogy: the pantry.
precise: dynamic random-access memory: each bit is stored as charge on a capacitor accessed through one transistor; reads are destructive and the charge leaks, so rows must be rewritten after reading and refreshed periodically.
source: D1 of F1-39 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-39 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an independent part of a DRAM chip that can work on one request while another bank works on another.
analogy: a pantry aisle with its own clerk.
precise: a two-dimensional array of cells with its own row decoder and sense amplifiers; operations to different banks can overlap.
source: D3 of F1-39 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach"); D1 of F1-39 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the one row of a bank that is currently "open" and can be read quickly.
analogy: the shelf pulled out onto the counter.
precise: the sense amplifiers of a bank, which hold the most recently activated row; column reads from the open row (row hits) avoid the activate step, while a different row requires precharge and activate (a row miss or conflict).
source: D3 of F1-39 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach"); D1 of F1-39 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an independent path between the processor and a group of memory modules.
analogy: a corridor with its own trolley.
precise: a data and command bus with its own controller logic and modules; channels operate in parallel, and consecutive blocks are commonly interleaved across them to add their bandwidth.
source: D3 of F1-39 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the processor that talks to DRAM.
analogy: the dispatcher who decides which order goes down which corridor and in which sequence.
precise: logic that maps physical addresses to channel, rank, bank, row and column, queues requests, schedules DRAM commands (often favouring row hits) and issues refreshes.
source: D3 of F1-39 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: some memory is "nearer" to some cores and faster for them.
analogy: two kitchens, each with its own pantry.
precise: non-uniform memory access: a shared-memory system in which memory is attached to several nodes (for example sockets), and a core's access to its own node's memory has lower latency and higher bandwidth than access to another node's memory over the interconnect.
source: D3 of F1-39 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach"); D8 of F1-39 (Linux kernel documentation and man-pages) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a new page is placed in the memory of the node whose core touches it first.
analogy: an ingredient is stored in the pantry of the kitchen that first asks for it.
precise: Linux's default NUMA placement: physical memory for a page is allocated, at its first page fault (F1-38), on the node of the CPU that faulted, unless a memory policy says otherwise.
source: D8 of F1-39 (Linux kernel documentation and man-pages) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
